As an S&C coach, you are probably aware of the story of [Milo of Croton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milo_of_Croton). Milo was a Greek athlete in the late 6th century BC who would begin an Olympic training cycle by carrying a newborn calf on his back everyday. Over time the calf would grow bigger and bigger, and Milo would grow stronger and stronger. Eventually he would be carrying a four year old cow on his back and he'd be in peak shape for the Olympics.[^1] What you probably didn't know, is that Milo's strength and conditioning coach was actually plotting his progress in Microsoft Excel the whole time. Of course, this was almost 3000 years ago, and just as training methods have progressed, so have our tools for analyzing data. This is why I've created this step-by-step guide to take you from an excel spreadsheet containing jump heights (or cow mass measurements) to a beautiful plot built using R, that will take your reports to the next level.

[^1]: Also: "He carried the full-grown cow the length of the stadium, then proceeded to kill, roast, and eat it." You can't make this stuff up.

## Who is this post for?

This post is for anyone who collects jump data with athletes/clients, and is at least somewhat familiar with using R and R Studio. A basic understanding of the [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) package will also be helpful.

Whether you have force plates and want to improve upon existing reporting solutions, or you want to visualize results obtained from a jump mat or phone application, I hope you will find this post useful or inspiring.

## Defining the Goal

Traditionally, as S&C coaches, we are interested in either the daily average or daily maximum jump height, but let's be greedy and try to include as much information in this plot as possible.

We want this plot to clearly show:

1.  Average Daily Jump Height

2.  Best Daily Jump

3.  The height of each jump performed

4.  Average performance across all 5 dates

That's a lot of information for one plot, so let's go one step at a time, and see if we can communicate all of this data in an aesthetically pleasing, non-cluttered plot.

## Getting Set Up

We will start by installing and loading all necessary packages.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(vroom)
library(janitor)
```
:::



For the purposes of this post, I've created a simple spreadsheet containing five days worth of CMJ results for a fictional athlete. You can access the file [here](https://github.com/AKates717/my-website/blob/master/Posts/2024-08-19-cmj-tracking1/recent_five.csv), or you can create your own in excel and read it into R Studio. The data can be loaded into the R Studio Environment using the `vroom` package, and assigned as a data-frame entitled `recent_five`.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
recent_five <- vroom("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AKates717/my-website/refs/heads/master/recent_five.csv")
```
:::

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

## Creating the Plot

### 1. Average Daily Jump Height

We will start by taking our `recent_five` data-frame, and creating a plot using the `ggplot` function.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = TRUE))) + #<1>
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), #<2>
               fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6) 
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Countermovement jump heights from the last five testing dates](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj1-1.png){#fig-cmj1 width=672}
:::
:::



1.  Using `factor()` results in equal spacing between dates, which improves readability
2.  Using `stat_summary()` allows us to do calculations within the layer of the plot, and saves us from creating more data-frames

If you are new to ggplot, this code reads:

> "Take the data in `recent_five` , create a plot with `Date` on the x-axis, then calculate the mean of `flight_height_tov` and plot it on the y-axis".

We now have a basic plot for our primary outcome measure; mean jump height.

Our next step is to add maximum jump height. But before we continue adding layers to the plot, let's customize the look of our plot.

### Brief Intermission: Improving plot aesthetics



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
#Create a custom theme for my plots and save it as ak_plot_theme

ak_plot_theme <- function(..., base_size = 12) {
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = base_size),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "black",
                              face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black",
                             face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust =0.6, vjust = 0.8),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16,
                              color = "black",
                              vjust = 5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "black",
                                 hjust = 0.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8,
                                face = "italic",
                                color = "black"),
    panel.grid.major =  element_line(color = "#e0e0e0"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff"),
    plot.background = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank())
}
```
:::



If you would like to view the custom theme I've created for this plot. You can un-hide the code above and copy the function `ak_plot_theme()` into your own R environment. The nuances of this theme are beyond the scope of this post, but you will see that I am going for a minimalist aesthetic.

Below is the updated code for our plot which includes adding some colour[^2], our custom theme, and improved labels. You can hover over the code annotations for more details. The new plot is displayed beside the old plot to highlight the differences.

[^2]: Solid Gold

    ![](austin-powers.gif)



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), 
               fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") + #<1>
  ak_plot_theme() + #<2>
  labs( #<3>
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)
```
:::



1.  The colour of the points has been changed to Gold using `colour = "#D19A2B"`.

2.  `ak_plot_theme()` has been added as a layer to the plot.

3.  Using `labs()`, y-axis label has been updated, x-axis label and plot title have been removed.



::: {#fig-cmj-2 .cell layout-ncol="2"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Old plot, no formatting](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj-2-1.png){#fig-cmj-2-1 width=672}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![New plot, nicely formatted](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj-2-2.png){#fig-cmj-2-2 width=672}
:::

Aesthetic improvements.
:::



### 2. Best Daily Jump Height

We'll add this layer in two steps.

[Step 1]{.underline}

Add a point to show the best (highest) jump our athlete performed each day. I've used `stat_summary()` again, but I've switched the function from ***mean*** to ***max***, and I've decreased the size of the points from 6 to 4, indicating that mean jump height is our primary outcome measure, and maximum jump height is a secondary outcome measure.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), 
               fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), #<<
               fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") + #<<
    ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Step 1 - Add a point for the best jump on each day.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj3-1.png){#fig-cmj3 width=672}
:::
:::



[Step 2]{.underline}

Add vertical lines connecting mean and max points. `Stat_summary` offers an argument called `fun.data` which allows you to compute multiple values at once. In this case, I've created a function called `mean_peak` which defines the mean and max values. I then pass this function to `fun.data` and use `geom="pointrange"` to draw the line.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#draw a line between the mean and the max jump height
mean_peak <- function(x) { #<<
  data.frame(y = (mean(x) + 0.0001), #<<
             ymax = max(x), #<<
             ymin = mean(x)) #<<
}

recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") + #<<
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Step 2 - Add vertical lines connecting mean and max.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj4-1.png){#fig-cmj4 width=672}
:::
:::



Lastly, I will add one additional `stat_summary()` layer using `geom="line"` to connect the daily mean scores with a line so we can see changes between daily scores a bit better.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") + #<<
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Connecting daily mean scores.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj5-1.png){#fig-cmj5 width=672}
:::
:::



### 3. Each Jump Performed

At this point, we've managed to display two different descriptive statistics in one nice clean plot. But like I said, we're being greedy here and we'd also like to see the height of every single jump. We'll add this data using a `geom_jitter` layer, which is basically just a `geom_point` that let's us spread the points out, making them a bit easier to see.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) + #<<
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Adding individual jump heights.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj6-1.png){#fig-cmj6 width=672}
:::
:::



### 4. Average performance across all five dates

Lastly, it would be helpful to know how each score compares to the overall mean for this athlete, so we'll add a horizontal line with the y-intercept set to the overall mean jump height.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) + #<<
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Our final plot... For now.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj7-1.png){#fig-cmj7 width=672}
:::
:::



## Next Steps

In this blog post I have given step-by-step instructions on how to create a unique plot to visualize CMJ data.

Although I am happy with the style of the plot, and the amount of information I have been able to include, there is one major flaw with the final product. Although we can see roughly where all of our data lines up with the y-axis, we have not communicated any actual values to our audience.

Picture it, you share your beautiful plot with a coach or athlete and their first question is: "How high did I jump?". If all you have is this plot, what are you going to tell them? In my next blog post, I will show you how to use `Plotly` to make our plot interactive, and to convey this vital information to our audience without ruining our minimalist aesthetic.

Thanks for reading!
